1.station: Reverse the last pitch roughly 15-20 m (about 50 ft) from the summit and work toward the Concord Tower side of the crest. The anchor is a tree carrying fixed slings, tucked off the crest near a shallow groove in the rock; two slung trees stand close together and the upper one is the sounder of the pair. It is much easier to pick out while leading pitch 4 than from above, so note it on the way up. The rappel lands on a sandy, tree-dotted ledge.
hazards: These trees are the only marker for the top of the descent and are easy to walk past on the summit ridge; a party that misses them commits itself to downclimbing the loose east gully instead.
The lower tree's slings are periodically found tired. Carry cord or webbing to replace rather than rappelling on whatever happens to be there.
Snow can linger on the landing ledge into early season.
1.pull: A hair over 30 m to the ledge, so a single 60 m rope arrives with almost nothing spare once it has stretched. Knot both ends.

2.station: Do not rappel straight on from the sandy ledge. Work right along the ledge, then down, then right again to reach a fixed station of bolts and chains on the steep wall. Parties consistently report this hardware as hard to spot, so scout it before pulling the first rope.
hazards: Loose sand and grit on the ledge above slabby downclimbing.
If the chains are not found after the ropes are pulled, the party is stranded between stations with no anchor.
2.pull: A plumb pull off bolts. Keep the strands clear of the ledge lip and its trees so nothing catches on the retrieve.

3.station: The lowest fixed station on the wall, straight below the previous one. The rappel from it runs slightly diagonally rather than plumb and finishes in the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at roughly 7,300 ft, close to where most parties leave packs at the top of the approach gully.
hazards: The line traverses, so anyone who loses the stance swings across the wall.
The notch and the gully below it are loose, and anything dislodged here funnels onto the climbers' path that other parties are walking up.
3.pull: Because the rappel is diagonal, the pull strand drags across the wall and this descent has a documented history of jammed ropes. One party had to fix one strand, lead back up the climbable ground to free it, then ascend to the station and re-rig. Feed the pull strand out and away from the diagonal, and pull from the notch rather than from directly under the anchor.

set.rappel_count_note: Three rappels on a single 60 m rope, which is the rope this route recommends and the configuration these three stations describe. Parties carrying two ropes combine the lower two into one double-rope rappel and descend in two, which is where the older count of 2 came from. Mountain Project also documents a variant that downclimbs the ridge and the 5.6 boulder problem, then follows the tree-filled gully east to a bolted station and reaches the ground in two single-rope rappels; that is a different set of stations from the tree-and-chains line described here, so do not mix the two. Individual lengths are not published; the first is reported as slightly over 30 m, and 30 m is the bound implied by three rappels on one 60 m rope rather than a measured figure. This is the standard descent line shared with the East Face and Northwest Face routes.

1.station: The three-bolt anchor on the serpentine summit block at the top of the climb. The rappel off it is short and awkward — a sit-and-spin start straight off the bolts — and drops the last pitch to a two-bolt station on a narrow ledge at the top of pitch 3. Break here even though the terrain below looks like it would go in one longer rappel.
hazards: A crack a couple of feet below the summit bolts is notorious for wedging rope. Stopping at the pitch-3 ledge instead of running the rope through to the top of pitch 2 is the accepted way to avoid it, and is the single most repeated warning on this descent.
Serpentine is slick rock, and slicker still when damp or dusty; the summit stance is small and the start of the rappel is over the edge rather than off a ledge.
1.pull: Pull from the ledge with the strands held out from the wall so neither end swings back into the crack under the summit anchor.

2.station: Two bolts on a narrow ledge at the top of pitch 3, replacing older pitons. From here the rappel reaches the large ledge with a slung boulder near the top of pitch 2. Party reports agree that a 60 m rope comes up about 5 m (15 ft) short of that ledge and that a 70 m only just makes it, so on a single 60 m most parties break the descent differently or downclimb the last few metres.
hazards: Coming up short leaves the rappeller hanging on a slick serpentine face above the ledge. Knot the ends and confirm the rope reaches before the last person commits.

A crack near the second slung boulder at the end of pitch 2 has wedged a rope end on the pull; the pitch is easy enough that one party simply scrambled back up to free it, but that is luck rather than a plan.
2.pull: This is the crack that eats ropes on this route. Walk the strands well out from the base of the wall before pulling, and pull briskly so the tail does not drop back in behind the boulder.

3.station: Rig from the slung boulder and fixed slings on the big ledge above pitch 2. These are natural anchors reinforced with webbing and are rebuilt periodically, so carry a few metres of spare cord rather than assuming the tat is fresh. The rappel lands on the base ledges and the class 3-4 gully where the climb started.
hazards: Slung-boulder and horn anchors are the weakest links on this descent and have been found tattered by arriving parties.
Below the last rappel the gully back down to the notch is class 3-4 and loose, with the approach talus and slabs beneath it.

set.rappel_count_note: The counts on this page assume different rope setups and are all correct. On two 60 m ropes it is three rappels: a double-rope rappel from the three-bolt summit anchor to the large ledge above pitch 2, then a short one to the top of pitch 1, then one more to the base ledges. On a single 60 m rope it is four, because a 60 m falls roughly 15 ft short of the pitch-2 ledge from the pitch-3 station. Two 70 m ropes reach mid-pitch-2 from the summit and allow a scramble to the top-of-pitch-1 anchor, dropping a rappel again. Whichever setup you carry, the strong recommendation from parties who have done it is to break the descent at the pitch-3 ledge rather than running one long rappel from the summit: a crack just under the summit bolts, and a second near the slung boulder at the end of pitch 2, are both documented rope-eaters.

1.station: Top station of the rappel line North Cascade Mountain Guides installed after the June 2022 rockfall: bolts and chains on a big ledge immediately above the small tree that older parties used to sling. All three new stations sit climber's right of the gully and off the line of ascent — skier's left as you face out on the way down — deliberately taking the descent out of the gully feature the route climbs. You reach it by downclimbing the arete's 3rd/4th-class ground plus one short, exposed 5th-class step.
hazards: A Mountaineers trip report found one of these bolted stations placed on a large block that is not attached to the mountain: counted from the bottom it is the third, which with three stations in place is this top one, above the gully. Inspect the rock the bolts are in, not only the hardware, and back it up if you are not satisfied.
The short 5th-class step above the station is exposed with real fall consequence. Stay roped, and place gear on it rather than soloing down.
1.pull: Built for a single 60 m rope, and the stations were placed to give steep, clean pulls clear of the gully.

2.station: Second of the three chain-and-bolt stations, on the ledge just above the chockstone, again set off to the side of the climbing line. Short sections of easy downclimbing link it to the station above, and how much you rappel versus downclimb is a party choice.
hazards: The gully immediately beside the line is the loose ground that produced the 2022 rockfall. Keep ropes and feet out of it — that is the whole reason this rappel line was moved.
This is a very popular route and stations back up on summer weekends; anything knocked loose lands on the party waiting below.
2.pull: Steep and fairly clean on a 60 m rope, provided the strands are kept out of the gully when you throw.

3.station: Lowest chain station. The rappel from it returns you to the base of the route, where the climbers' trail leads back down through talus and slabs alongside the stream to the Blue Lake Trail.
hazards: Talus and slabs immediately below the last station, with the pull zone directly above anyone still coiling ropes.

The alternative descent some parties take instead — traversing to the Southwest Couloir and walking it out — avoids rope work but is loose and can hold firm snow well into summer, so it is not automatically the safer option without an axe.

set.rappel_count_note: Three stations, all installed by North Cascade Mountain Guides after the June 2022 rockfall and all placed climber's right of the gully and off the climbing line so the pulls are clean and nothing is knocked onto parties on the route. The line was designed around a single 60 m rope; sources describe reaching the base in two to three rappels because how much of the connecting ground you downclimb rather than rappel is a party choice, not a difference in rope setup. The old station was a small tree in the gully — it sits just below the new top anchor and is superseded, not part of this sequence.

1.station: This route does not have its own rappel line: after topping out you downclimb the South Arete, and the stations are the ones North Cascade Mountain Guides installed there after the June 2022 rockfall. The top anchor is bolts and chains on a big ledge immediately above the small tree older parties used to sling, set climber's right of the gully and off the climbing line. Reaching it means 3rd/4th-class downclimbing plus one short, exposed 5th-class step.
hazards: A Mountaineers trip report found one of these bolted stations placed on a large detached block — the third counting up from the bottom, which with three stations in place is this top one, above the gully. Check the rock, not just the bolts.
The 5th-class step on the downclimb above the station is exposed; parties newer to alpine terrain should stay roped for it.
1.pull: Designed around a single 60 m rope, with steep clean pulls kept out of the gully.

2.station: Second chain-and-bolt station on the South Arete line, on the ledge just above the chockstone, off to the side of the climbing line.
hazards: The gully alongside is the loose ground the 2022 rockfall came from; keeping ropes and bodies out of it is the reason this line exists.
Queues at the stations are common on summer weekends, which puts a party directly under your rope pull.

3.station: Lowest chain station, returning you to the base of the wall and the climbers' trail down to the Blue Lake Trail. If you parked at the hairpin rather than the Blue Lake trailhead, plan the road walk or shuttle from here.
hazards: Loose talus and slabs under the last station.
Rope pull lands on anyone still sorting gear at the base.

set.rappel_count_note: Three rappels on a single 60 m rope, but they are not this route's own stations — the descent downclimbs the South Arete and uses the three bolt-and-chain stations North Cascade Mountain Guides installed there after the June 2022 rockfall, which are shared with the South Arete, Southwest Rib and other South Early Winters Spire routes. Sources give the South Arete descent as two to three rappels because the connecting ground can be downclimbed instead; three is the number of fixed stations. Lengths here are inferred from the single 60 m rope the line was built for, not measured.

1.station: Finding this anchor is the real crux of the descent — it cannot be seen from the summit. From the summit block move onto the western side and scramble down and across one narrow, tricky, exposed step to the top of the North Face; the station does not come into view until you are a few feet from it. The Mountaineers describe it as three good bolts with hangers and no chains, Mountain Project as chains atop the North Face, so expect that it may have been rebuilt and judge what is actually there.
hazards: The traverse to reach the station is exposed scrambling that most parties do unroped.

The rappel goes over a sharp lip straight onto vertical face. Parties have called it the mental crux of the whole climb. Get the rope onto the least sharp part of the edge and have the transition over the lip rehearsed before the first person commits.
One party found a leg of the anchor cord running directly through a hanger. Re-rig rather than accept it.
1.pull: It is possible to skip a station with a double-length rappel from the summit, and it is a bad idea: the first ledge below is blocky and loose, ropes jam there readily, and going back up to free one showers the notch with rock. Wind is a real factor on this face — one party had a strand blown into a crack about 15 m (50 ft) off the descent line and had to detour to retrieve it, so lower the ends in a saddlebag rather than throwing them on a breezy day.

2.station: The next of a series of ledges below the sharp lip, each carrying a slung rappel anchor. This is the station a 50 m rope only just reaches, which is why 60 m is the near-universal recommendation.
hazards: On a 50 m rope you arrive on the knots. Knot the ends regardless.
The ledges here are blocky and hold loose rock that goes down the fall line onto the notch and the approach gully.
2.pull: Keep the strands off the blocky ledge edges — this is the terrain where ropes on this descent are documented to stick.

3.station: Lowest of the slung ledge stations. The rappel from it lands on downclimbable low-5th and 4th-class ground just above the high notch between Kangaroo Temple and Little Finger where the route starts. Some parties skip the last one or two rappels here and simply downclimb back to the col.
hazards: The scramble from the last rappel down into the notch is loose, and the approach gully below it is the line other parties climb.
This is a popular club route; expect a queue at the stations on weekends and keep helmets on while waiting.

set.rappel_count_note: Three single-rope rappels on a 60 m rope is the standard sequence and the one these stations describe. The same descent goes in two on two 50 m ropes, which is where the lower count comes from — same line, different rope setup, not a disagreement. A 50 m single rope only barely reaches the second station, so 60 m is strongly preferred. Skipping a station with a double-length rappel from the summit is possible but is warned against: the first ledge is blocky and loose, ropes stick there, and retrieving one brings rock down. Sources also disagree on the hardware at the top anchor — three bolts with hangers and no chains per The Mountaineers, chains per Mountain Project — so inspect what is in place rather than planning around either.

1.station: Rap chains on the summit, reached from the true summit by a short, awkward step and slither over the top of the summit block; trip reports note a small tree beside the top anchor as well. On two ropes this becomes one double-rope rappel that reaches the ledge above pitch 1 in a single go, which is why the same descent is described as three rappels by some parties and two by others.
hazards: The move from the summit onto the anchor is short but exposed and clumsy in boots or with a pack on.
This face stays wet after rain and can be icy early and late in the season, and the rappel stances are where that is felt.
1.pull: Set the middle mark carefully if you are running the full double-rope version — parties who combine the top two rappels report it as a full-length pull with nothing spare.

2.station: Bolted chain anchor on the climbing line just below the 5.0 slab section of pitch 3. The rappel from it drops to the bushy, tree-dotted ledge at the top of pitch 1.
hazards: The landing ledge is vegetated and the brush catches rope ends on both the throw and the pull.
Slab above the station stays greasy after rain.

3.station: The station on the bushy pitch-1 ledge, from which the last rappel returns you to the base of the climb at the Liberty Bell-Concord notch. Do not plan on this one being fixed hardware: the published claim that the whole line is bolts and chains with no natural gear needed is contradicted by parties on the ground, one of whom recorded rappelling off webbing on the tree here, and another whose anchor at this level was a small bush that held under testing but was plainly not bomber.
hazards: A tree or bush anchor rather than fixed hardware — this is the one station on the descent where you may have to build or replace, so carry webbing and a rap ring.
The rappel lands at the notch, which is the top of the loose approach gully every party climbing Liberty Bell and Concord walks up. Anything dislodged goes straight down it.
3.pull: Pull well out from the notch so the strands come down clear of the brush on the ledge above.

set.rappel_count_note: Three single-rope rappels on one 60 m rope is the standard North Face descent and is what these stations describe; parties carrying two ropes combine the top two into one double-rope rappel and reach the notch in two, which is the same line with a different rope setup rather than a different descent. The claim that the whole line is bolts and chains with no natural gear required is not accurate: a Mountaineers party recorded webbing on the tree for part of it, and another reported a bush as the anchor at that level, so carry webbing and a ring. Keep this distinct from the South Face descent used when linking Concord with Lexington — that is a separate two-rappel line of roughly 30 m each with its own bolted mid-face station, and its stations must not be mixed with these.

1.station: Rap rings set back from the summit at the top of pitch 7. The rappel runs diagonally down to the anchor at the base of pitch 7, which is the pattern for the whole descent: the rap line sits roughly 3-5 m (10-15 ft) skier's left of the bolted climbing line the entire way down.
hazards: There is an edge right at the start. It has since been ground down, but put the rope over the least sharp part of it anyway.
Loose rock sits on several of the belay ledges on this route; stack ropes so you are not sweeping it off onto the party below.
1.pull: Nothing on this descent pulls plumb, because the anchors zigzag left of the bolts. Flick the strands clear of the bolt line before pulling or they hang up on hardware.

2.station: Rappel down the face to an anchor set about 3 m left of and 3 m above the top of the dihedral. Do not stop at the top of the dihedral itself — the anchor you want is above and left of it.
hazards: Throw the rope slightly left of the bolt line: climbers coming up are directly beneath, and rope thrown down the line takes loose rock with it.

3.station: A short rappel to the anchor on the ledge beside the dihedral pitch. The last part of it hangs free above the ledge, so expect a spin before your feet find anything.
hazards: Free-hanging finish onto a ledge — control the swing rather than arriving sideways.
Loose rock on the ledge.

4.station: Two anchors exist at the pitch 4 stance. Take the skier's-left one; the right-hand option puts your ropes across the climbing line.
hazards: Choosing the right-hand anchor drops your ropes onto anyone climbing, which is why the left is the published preference.

5.station: The station people miss, and the one that matters most. Push through the cedar bushes directly below the anchor above, rappel the low-angle upper part of pitch 3, and aim for a tree about 3 m tall standing roughly 5 m skier's left of the climbing line. The intermediate anchor is tucked into a nook just below that tree.
hazards: Missing this station and continuing down the vertical face below it leaves a party on a single rope unable to reach the next anchors. This is the one place on the descent where a route-finding error strands you mid-face, and the route description flags it explicitly.
The cedar bushes hide both the anchor and the rope; do not rappel past on autopilot because the terrain is low-angle here.
5.pull: Two ropes make the consequence of missing the nook recoverable; on a single rope it is not.

6.station: From the nook anchor, down the vertical face of lower pitch 3 to the large ledge at the pitch 2 anchors. Take the left anchor if it is free.
hazards: This is the steep face the previous warning is about — you are now committed below the nook.
Loose rock on the large ledge.

7.station: Drops to the pitch 1 rappel anchor, which is about 3 m below and 3-5 m skier's left of the pitch 1 belay bolts — not the belay itself.
hazards: Easy to arrive at the belay rather than the rap station and burn time traversing across on a slabby stance.

8.station: Last rappel to the start of the route. The starting ledge is several hundred feet above the ground and genuinely exposed, so this is not a place to untie casually.
hazards: The base ledge is exposed above a long drop. Stay roped, walk back to the belay bolt and pull the rope from there rather than coming off the system on the ledge.
Keep helmets on: on a route this popular there is usually still a party above you when you land.
In spring the approach gully below still holds steep snow, which complicates the walk back to the Sunrise Mine Trail after the last rappel.

set.rappel_count_note: Eight single-strand rappels off fixed bolted anchors, and a single 60 m rope is documented as sufficient for every one of them (a 70 m gives more margin). Two 60 m ropes also work and are the recommended insurance for one specific reason: if you miss the intermediate anchor in the nook below the small tree on rap 5 and continue down the vertical face, a single-rope party cannot reach the next anchors. The rap line is not the climbing line — it stays roughly 3-5 m skier's left of the bolts for the whole descent, so anchors are found left of where you climbed and pulls are never plumb.

1.station: From the bunny-ears notch at the top of the route, downclimb about 5 m (15 ft) to the next ledge down. The anchor is fixed slings around a large granite horn — a natural anchor, not hardware. The rappel from it runs on doubled 60 m ropes to a second large slung horn at the top of pitch 2.
hazards: The downclimb from the notch to the horn crosses loose blocks and broken corners; it is short but it is where the descent's rockfall risk is concentrated.
The station is whatever tat is currently around the horn. Carry webbing and a ring so you can replace rather than rappel on faded slings.
1.pull: Two 60 m ropes are the standard kit for this descent and a single rope will not link these two stations. Pull the strands clear of the horn so they do not wrap it.

2.station: The large slung horn at the top of pitch 2 — the same kind of natural station as the first, and the one you land on from above. The second doubled rappel from it returns you to the scree at the base of the East Face.
hazards: Second natural horn anchor with no fixed hardware; inspect and back up before the last person goes.
Loose rock across the face means anything the ropes sweep off lands at the base of the route where packs and other parties are.
2.pull: Straight down the face to the scree; stand out from the base of the wall when pulling.

set.rappel_count_note: Two rappels, and this count assumes two 60 m ropes doubled through natural horn anchors — that is the published kit for the route and a single rope does not link the stations. Both anchors are slung granite horns rather than fixed hardware, so carry replacement webbing. Per-station distances are not published in any source found; the values on file are estimates from the description of the first rappel as roughly a 120 ft double-rope rappel and should not be planned around.
